title: New contracts after an agreement grew by half or ran two years long
question: When an agreement grew by half or more, or ran two years past its first end date, did the same department then give the contractor new contracts, how were they awarded, and how soon?
finding: 139 contractor-and-department pairs had such an agreement at least a year ago and can be followed in the contract table (31 more contractors could not be found there under the name the Board title uses). 87 of them (63%) were given new contracts by the same department afterwards: 332 contracts with ceilings of $5.73 billion, the first typically 508 days later. By the purchasing rule keyed on them, 204 were competed, 99 were not ($1.61 billion) and 29 carry a rule that does not say. For comparison, among 124 pairs whose agreement neither grew by a quarter nor ran a year long, 60% were given new contracts afterwards. Leaving nonprofits out, the figures are 51% of 79 after an overrun and 53% of 88 without one. The most new work followed APX Inc. (Public Utilities Commission): 4 new contracts, $1.35 billion. An agreement that grew is not a bar to new work, and nothing in the files suggests it is treated as one.
how: An overrun here is a Board-approved agreement whose ceiling reached half again its first amount, or whose end date moved two years or more past the first; the date it crossed that line is the date the Board passed the amendment that did it. One row per contractor and department (the largest rise where there are several), only where at least a year has passed since and the name in the Board title is a supplier name in the contract table (a title that shortens or lengthens a name is matched to the one supplier whose name begins or ends with it). New contracts are rows of the Supplier Contracts table for the same contractor and the same department with a start date after that day and a ceiling above zero, leaving out the grown agreement itself. "Competed" and "not competed" come from the purchasing rule keyed on each new contract (emergency, sole source, bidding waived by ordinance and other "not bid" rules count as not competed; rules that do not say are "unclear"). Where a Board title names no department, new contracts from any department are counted.
limits: Growth in these agreements is mostly a service renewed, and a department that renews a provider will naturally also sign new agreements with it; the comparison group is smaller, differently mixed and not a controlled test. Large providers hold many contracts whether or not one of them grew. A new contract number can be the same service put out to competition again and won by the incumbent. The purchasing rule is keyed by the department and "unclear" is common for grants. What would turn a row into a finding is a performance record. For construction the Administrative Code requires one, a contractor evaluation database, and the Budget and Legislative Analyst found it all but unused (see the official findings). Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
